newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo managers urge revision of '97 growth targets.
newsitem.headline: Yugo managers urge revision of '97 growth targets.

text.p: Yugoslav managers on Wednesday said positive economic results for the start of the year were misleading and called for a revision of 1997 growth forecasts, which they said were too ambitious.

"I think the economy is heading down a well, so what is the use of showing positive indicators," Momcilo Jevdjovic of Grafopromet Cacak told a meeting of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce Economic Committee.

At the present low industry capacity utilisation, estimated at around 50 percent of levels before the breakup of the former Yugoslav federation in 1991, it is questionable how successful and encouraging the early 1997 results are, Jevdjovic said.
According to official statistics, industry output in the first two months rose 5.1 percent on the same period in 1996, and year-on-year growth in February stood at 7.8 percent.
The highest growth of 256 percent was in ferrous metallurgy followed by the oil derivatives industry with 254.7 percent.

Trade was worth $917 million, or 45 percent up on the same period last year, with exports rising 48.9 percent to $283 million and imports by 43.3 percent to $634 million. The January-February trade deficit stood at $351 million.
The government target for 1997 was 13.9 percent growth in industrial output, six percent in agriculture, 13 percent in GDP, 42 percent in exports and 20 percent in imports.
"Export growth in the first two months of the year is almost at the planned level," said Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce official Milija Mihajlovic.
The chamber said results at the start of 1997 were "encouraging", with prices and the dinar exchange rate stable, mainly thanks to restrictive credit-monetary policy.
But dropping wages and employment, growing insolvency and lack of working capital remain burdens on the economy, preventing more dynamic growth, Mihajlovic said.
Petar Drobnjakovic of the Priboj FAP Famos truck factory said positive industrial data could not be viewed separately from negative figures on wages, employment and liquidity.
The managers called for a study on which branches were in the biggest crisis and which had the greatest propulsion and prospects of becoming the backbone of economic growth.
While metal processing and machine building have shown the highest growth, they are also in the most difficult situation, together with construction.

"Adequate measures must be taken to help these industries, which employ more than 500,000 of the estimated 2.4 million workforce, otherwise we will lose whole and very strong industries," Drobnjakovic said.
Producers who were among top exporters before sanctions were imposed on Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, in 1992, must be helped to renew these ties, he said.
The managers agreed the state should do more to protect local industry and not liberalise trade "merely for the sake of liberalisation."

"There is anarchy and complete lack of hearing for the industry's needs and how to revive production," Drobnjakovic said, criticising the state's liberal approach to imports of certain goods which could be produced on the local market.
"Why do we roll out the red carpet for their (foreign) imports and a bed of thorns for our own exports?" said Bozidar Batizic of the Zeljezara Niksic steel works.
Compared with 1989, the 1996 results are a catastrophe and the economy is lagging far behind other former Yugoslav republics and neighbouring countries, he said.

"The economy should be viewed as a chain. We cannot treat branches of industry separately. We must consider what will happen to the others if we were to let one link drop out overnight," Batizic said.
-- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
